title: Where Muslims differ
hookLine: some embrace orders and saints' shrines, others hold these as later additions, and all say keep to the Qur'an

lines: A WHITE DOME, A GREEN CLOTH.
cards: Friday, just after the prayer. A family drives out to a saint's tomb, a white dome with green cloth over the grave.
They recite al-Fatiha for him, ask God for help near the resting place of a man they love, and give food to the poor at the gate. Their cousins, just as devout, would never go.
They'd say, with conviction, that this isn't how the Prophet and his companions practiced, and that prayer should be directed to God alone, with nothing that looks like a go-between.
Two weeks on the Sufi path, and now, honestly: where Muslims differ.

teach.h: FOR CENTURIES, PART OF THE MAINSTREAM.
teach.b: For many centuries, Sufism sat inside the mainstream of Muslim learning. Great scholars of law, like al-Ghazali, were Sufis.
Across the Ottoman lands, South Asia, West Africa and Southeast Asia, the orders were part of ordinary life, and visiting the shrines of saints was common. In many places, it still is.
Other Muslims have long criticized parts of it.

teach.h: IBN TAYMIYYAH AND THE SALAFI CRITIQUE.
teach.b: The medieval scholar Ibn Taymiyyah respected early Sufis like Junayd, but condemned practices at graves that he believed compromised tawhid, the oneness of God.

Modern Salafi movements, which aim to follow the salaf, the first generations of Muslims, hold that orders, shrine visits and musical sama' are later additions, bid'ah; some reject tasawwuf as a separate path altogether.
Others stand in between: they value tasawwuf as purifying the heart, and question some practices. Shia Muslims visit the shrines of the Prophet's family, and their relation to the Sufi orders varies.
These are real differences, sometimes painful ones. But every side argues from the Qur'an and the sunnah.

teach.h: REFER IT TO ALLAH AND THE MESSENGER.
teach.b: The Qur'an tells believers, when they dispute, in Pickthall's words, to "refer it to Allah and the messenger."

And a hadith in al-Bukhari says a judge who does his best and gets it right has two rewards, and one who does his best and gets it wrong still has one. Scholars read it as covering any qualified jurist.
Disagreement, in Arabic ikhtilaf, is old in Islam.

how: Muslims differ on Sufi orders, visiting saints' shrines and music in worship: some embrace them, Salafi Muslims and others reject them as later additions, and others take a middle position, while all appeal to the Qur'an and the sunnah.

o: a split that divides Muslims into two sects
a ruling that every scholar has agreed on

games.q: two devout Muslims disagree about visiting a saint's shrine. what does the Qur'an tell believers to do when they dispute?
o: refer it to Allah and the messenger.
games.why: refer it to Allah and the messenger (4:59). both sides argue from the Qur'an and the sunnah.

practice: In your mind, sit with the family at the shrine and understand why it moves them; then sit with the cousins and understand why it worries them.
You don't have to decide: hold both with respect for a few breaths, then try the same with someone in your own family you disagree with. If you pray, you can pray for both.

wordCard.voice: Ikhtilaf. Difference, disagreement among scholars — the old, recognized name for where Muslims differ on orders, shrines and music. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: difference, disagreement among scholars; an old, recognized part of Islamic learning.

carryVoice: Your line: the same Qur'an underneath. Differences and all, one Book. That's day three hundred seven.
